description: I’m an independent participant passionate about AI, space science, and environmental problem-solving. I’m developing EarthShield AI, a project that combines NASA satellite data, weather information, and AI-powered analysis to help understand natural hazards such as wildfires, floods, cyclones, and droughts. My goal is to turn Earth data into actionable insights for a safer, more resilient planet.
summary:
EarthShield AI: Turning Earth Data into Actionable Environmental Insights

EarthShield AI is an AI-powered environmental intelligence platform developed to make Earth observation data more accessible, understandable, and useful. It integrates NASA satellite imagery and Earth observation datasets with weather information to monitor and analyze four major environmental hazards: wildfires, floods, cyclones, and droughts.

The platform provides an interactive map, real-time and updated environmental data where available, hazard indicators, data visualizations, and AI-powered explanations. These features help users explore environmental conditions, interpret scientific data, and better understand potential risks.

EarthShield AI addresses the challenge of transforming complex Earth science data into meaningful insights. Natural hazards can threaten communities, ecosystems, infrastructure, and livelihoods. By combining NASA's open data, geospatial technology, weather information, and artificial intelligence, the project aims to improve environmental awareness, support preparedness, and contribute to more informed decision-making for a safer and more resilient planet.
details:
Project Details: EarthShield AI

What does it do or how does it work?
EarthShield AI is an interactive environmental intelligence dashboard that visualizes real-time satellite, meteorological, and natural event data. The application aggregates data from multiple sources (including NASA GIBS, FIRMS, EONET, and POWER) and uses the Nemotron 3.5 AI model to generate plain-language insights. It operates through several dedicated layers:

  • Satellite Natural View (Precipitation): Displays live rainfall data using a color-coded system: Green indicates light rain, Yellow and Orange show moderate to heavy rainfall, and Red represents the heaviest downpours.
  • Data Transparency: If a user selects the "Natural image with missing scan lines" view, visible gaps appear on the map. These gaps represent areas where the NASA satellite could not scan or collect data, ensuring transparency rather than faking continuous data.
  • Greenery Index: Tracks vegetation health over an 8-day period. Higher color intensity reflects denser or healthier vegetation. Users can compare this index directly with rainfall data to see how precipitation impacts local plant growth.
  • Thermal Anomaly Detection: Users can detect thermal anomalies within a 50 to 200-kilometer radius.
  • Weather & Event Analysis: By selecting a location, users can analyze local weather patterns (using NASA POWER and OpenWeather) and track nearby natural events (via NASA EONET), receiving detailed AI insights from Nemotron 3.5.

What benefits does it have?
EarthShield AI makes complex Earth observation data accessible to everyone. By integrating NASA EONET, users can track natural events (like storms, wildfires, or volcanic activity) in real time. NASA POWER provides reliable meteorological and solar data, which, when combined with visual layers, offers a comprehensive environmental picture. The app doesn't just show data; it uses Nemotron 3.5 to explain what that data means for the selected location, making climate science understandable for farmers, researchers, and everyday citizens.

What is the intended impact of the project?
The intended impact is to democratize climate and disaster data. By allowing users to easily spot thermal anomalies and heavy rainfall (red zones) within a 50–200 km radius, the app aids in rapid disaster response. It also fosters climate awareness by visually demonstrating the direct correlation between rainfall and vegetation health over an 8-day period. Showing "missing scan lines" is a deliberate choice to educate users about the realities and limitations of satellite telemetry.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Frontend/Backend: Next.js (React framework) with server-side API routes.
  • AI Model: Nemotron 3.5 (for natural language generation and data explanation).
  • APIs: NASA GIBS (satellite imagery), NASA FIRMS (thermal anomalies), NASA EONET (natural events), NASA POWER (meteorological data), and OpenWeather (local weather).
  • Hosting & Deployment: Vercel (using server-side environment variables to secure API keys).
  • Data Handling: Environment variables (.env) ensure sensitive credentials are never exposed to the client-side.

How is your project creative?
Our creativity lies in the "Explainable Data" approach. Instead of just displaying a heatmap, we use the Nemotron 3.5 AI model to interpret multi-layered environmental data. Displaying the "missing scan lines" breaks the illusion of perfect data, teaching users about satellite telemetry. Combining thermal anomaly radar, rainfall/precipitation views, an 8-day vegetation index, and EONET natural event tracking creates a unique, multi-layered environmental storytelling tool that goes far beyond a standard weather app.

What factors did your team consider?

  • API Reliability: We considered that some APIs (like NASA GIBS) work without keys, while others (FIRMS, EONET, POWER, and the Nemotron 3.5 model) require them. We built the app to handle API failures gracefully, showing error messages rather than silently faking data.
  • Security: We chose Vercel specifically because it supports server-side environment variables, ensuring our API keys are never exposed in the browser.
  • AI Model Selection: We selected Nemotron 3.5 to ensure reliable, high-quality AI responses and to avoid the quota and access limitations we previously encountered with other models.
  • User Experience: We ensured a clear distinction between "Live Mode" (real-time data) and "Demo Mode" (fallback data), and explicitly labeled them so users are never confused about what they are looking at.
